abstract: Genes implicated in brain disorders have diverse functions, but how altered dosage shapes their effects on developmental cell fate remains unclear. In a cell-state dynamics model of the developing human brain, genes expressed earlier in development responded more strongly to knockout than to overexpression, and this dosage dominance tracked neuronal-glial fate. Fate responses of 14,044 genes formed 31 modules across 21 lineages. Stronger perturbations could reverse fate responses despite correlated predicted expression changes across neuronal destinations. Disease-risk genes occupied shared and distinct developmental programs. Within autism, module timing distinguished genes associated with and without intellectual disability or developmental delay, while de novo and common variation implicated different modules. Knockout signatures of selected autism-associated modules matched the neuronal-down, glial-up pattern that postmortem autism cortex shares with other psychiatric disorders. These findings connect heterogeneous genetic risk through developmental programs whose fate responses depend on dosage and cellular context.
